feedback: If a child names the organ but not what it detects, prompt: 'Your eyes — but what do eyes pick up?' (light) and 'Your ears pick up…?' (sound).
If a child leaves out touch/skin, hand them the feely-bag object: 'What is your skin telling you — can you name two things, like bumpy, cold, or wet?'
Confirm correct triples by repeating them back: 'Yes — nose, smell, you smelled the flowers.'
activities.intendedInsight: Each sense uses a particular body part to detect a different kind of information about the world.
learnerActions: Visit hands-on stations and USE each sense before naming it: a feely bag (reach in and feel without looking), sound jars or a listening game, smell pots, a taste tray, and spot-it pictures.
After each station, say three things aloud: the sense used, the body part (organ) that detected it, and WHAT it picked up — e.g. 'touch, my skin, it felt bumpy and cold'.
Match five cards that pair each sense to its organ and to an everyday example: eyes catch a rainbow, ears catch a barking dog, skin feels warm sand, tongue tastes lemon, nose smells baking.
activities.title: Sense stations: use it, then name it

feedback: If a child predicts the tongue alone will manage and is surprised, name it: 'The flavour faded because smell helps taste — they team up.'

If a child says taste and smell are the same sense, separate them: the nose detects smells (odours in the air), the tongue detects tastes like sweet, sour, salty and bitter; together they make the full flavour of food, but they are different senses.
Link to daily life: 'That's why an orange tastes boring when you have a very blocked-up nose with a cold.'
activities.intendedInsight: Taste and smell cooperate: much of flavour comes from smell, so for flavour the tongue does not do the job by itself — these two senses combine to build the taste you recognise. (This is about flavour specifically; other senses can still work on their own.)
learnerActions: Before tasting, predict: 'If I pinch my nose shut, will I still tell these two flavours apart?' Say why you think so.
Taste two foods with the same texture but different flavours (e.g. two jellybean flavours, or finely grated apple and pear) with the nose pinched, then again with the nose open, and compare.
Say what changed and which two senses were working together.
activities.title: Senses team up: the nose-hold taste test

feedback: If a child expects a specific zone, invite them to test the same flavour on another part: 'Can you still taste it here?'
Affirm the corrected idea and tie it back: 'Taste buds all around your tongue can pick up every kind of taste — there are no special zones. Taste is one of our five senses.'
activities.intendedInsight: The old 'tongue map' (separate zones for each taste) is a myth: taste buds on the tip, sides and back of the tongue can each pick up all the basic tastes. The middle has fewer taste buds, so tastes can feel weaker there.
learnerActions: Taste a strong flavour (e.g. something sour or salty) touched to different parts of the tongue, such as the tip and each side.
Notice whether you can taste the same flavour in each place you tried, not just in one 'zone'.
State the myth and the correction in your own words: 'There are no separate zones for each taste.'
activities.title: Tongue-map myth buster
